source_terms: naturalism and other pictorial technologies served to reconfigure or recontextualize existing forms and thereby expand the domain of commodity address
item.claim: Jain argues that the deployment of new image-making techniques, including technological mass reproduction and elements of Western naturalism, "helped mass-manufactured images to forge an arena of common address across varying social constituencies — that is, to 'naturalize' an expanded category of the popular." Her worked case is M. V. Dhurandhar's 1932 Woodward's Gripe Water calendar, which she reads as deploying two distinct registers of signification at once: a perspectival, narrative, allegorical register aimed at a modernising Indian and European resident elite, and an indexical, frontal, iconic register that institutes a divine presence. She states the general point: "commodity aesthetics provided a ground for reformulations of community and locality, in this case by drawing colonial residents and the Indian elite into a common frame of address," driven by "the opposing expansive and conservative imperatives of mass production: to solicit the largest possible audience while also drawing on familiar frames of reference."
item.interpretation_basis: The reading of the Dhurandhar calendar as doubled in address, and the generalisation from it to the expansive function of naturalism, are Jain's. She advances the position explicitly against accounts that treat Indian popular aesthetics as an iconic realm resistant to Western naturalism.

mechanism.text: Mass production pulls in two directions at once: it must reach as many people as possible, and it must remain legible within frames those people already hold. A single artefact that carries two registers can satisfy both, addressing constituencies that would otherwise require separate artefacts — which is why technique expansion and audience expansion travel together.

scope.conditions: Indian commercial imagery from roughly the 1880s to the mid-twentieth century. Jain marks the Dhurandhar case as exceptional — "it represents something of an aberration, a path not taken" — because the constituency it addressed did not last.

caveats.text: the central worked example is one the author calls an aberration and a path not taken. The mechanism is argued from a case she says did not persist, which is unusual and should be visible to anyone using the object
'expanded the domain of commodity address' is an interpretation of a historical pattern; no measure of reach, sales or audience composition is presented anywhere
Jain is arguing against Pinney's and Rajadhyaksha's readings by name. The object records her position in a disagreement among specialists, not a settled result

source_terms: The signature campaign used 'doodh' musically to make milk sound cool and aspirational.
item.claim: In the NDDB Operation Flood frames reproduced here, the sung word "doodh" is set typographically as the picture itself — repeated four times in a heavy rounded yellow display face against black, beside the singer — rather than appearing as a caption or subtitle under a scene. The second frame shows a glass of milk with the Operation Flood mark and a cartoon buffalo.
item.interpretation_basis: The source's caption says the campaign used "doodh" musically. That the word is rendered as the frame's principal visual element, rather than as supporting text, is the extractor's observation from the plate. The mechanism proposed for it is likewise the extractor's and is not the source's: typesetting the sung word as the image binds the audio and the visual to the same token, so the frame remains legible with the sound off and the jingle remains attributable with the picture unseen.

scope.conditions: India; a national dairy development campaign; frames only, no date given in this source

the sound-off / picture-unseen reasoning is the extractor's inference and is not in the source

source_terms: But I would submit that the Airtel ad was a depiction of a future, not the current reality. And in a sense, good advertising is an attempt to always stay one step ahead of the consumer.
It is possibly true that in most Indian homes, the woman is the homemaker and the man is the breadwinner.
item.claim: Discussing a 2014 Airtel commercial in which a woman manager's subordinate turns out to be her husband, the author states plainly that the advertisement depicted a future rather than a current reality, and that in most Indian homes the older division of roles still held. What an advertisement shows is therefore evidence about what an advertiser judged aspirational, not evidence about how common the depicted arrangement was.

mechanism.text: The author holds that good advertising deliberately runs one step ahead of the consumer, so a depiction is selected for its aspirational pull, which decouples it from prevalence.

scope.conditions: India, 2014; argued from one commercial and generalised by the author

caveats.text: 'good advertising is an attempt to always stay one step ahead of the consumer' is the author's practitioner aphorism, not a tested rule, and it is offered without any account of how far ahead is too far
the author notes the same ad drew opposite readings — praised as an ode to the new Indian woman, criticised for still placing the woman at the stove — and he declines to adjudicate

source_stated_problems: an advertisement's depiction of a social arrangement can be mistaken for evidence that the arrangement is common

intra_source_relations.note: the strongest internal brake on reading campaigns as social measurement

provenance.locator: Ch. 'Jo Biwi Se Kare Pyaar…', Airtel passage (spine 9)

source_terms: Advertisers have at times used social consciousness as a tool to further the aims of commerce.
Tata Tea managed to blend in a very relevant social message along with its core message of refreshing tea.
item.claim: The source records a recurring Indian pattern in which advertisers attach a social cause to a commercial message: Amul's advertising celebrating the milk co-operative movement, Tata Steel's "We also make steel", and Tata Tea's "Jaago Re" (2008), which asked Indians to raise awareness of social causes and was refreshed in 2014 as "Power of 49" urging women to vote. The author states the commercial purpose plainly — social consciousness used "as a tool to further the aims of commerce".

scope.conditions: India; named campaigns dated 2008 and 2014, others undated

caveats.text: the author does not claim these campaigns produced either social or commercial outcomes; no measurement is offered for either

he separately records the counter-case: a 2015 Kalyan jewellery execution showing a dark-skinned child fanning a film star drew criticism for child labour and colour discrimination and was withdrawn with an apology. Social framing is not automatically favourably received

source_stated_problems: a brand adopting a social position can be read as exploiting it

provenance.section: Jaago Re and the Kalyan counter-case
provenance.locator: Introduction (spine 4), Ch. 'The Tingling Freshness of Teens' (spine 8), Ch. 'No Squeeze…' (spine 32)

item.claim: Bijapurkar proposes a segmentation whose axis is not spending power but VALUE ORIENTATION — how a buyer thinks about benefit against cost. Her five: the rich as benefit maximizers, oriented to "money for value", willing to pay more for more, described as "anywhere in the world consumers who just happen to be in India"; the consuming class as cost-benefit optimizers, oriented to "value for money", balancing the two continuously, "very hard to seduce with imagery-oriented brand benefits"; the climbers as cash-constrained benefit maximizers with a fixed price point who shop for the maximum available within it; the aspirants, new and therefore occasional consumers; and the destitute. She claims the model is generic — "this value orientation-based consumer class model is a generic Indian model that works for all businesses" — and demonstrates it across office automation, hospital services, cellphones, education, chemicals and farm equipment.

mechanism.text: Two buyers with the same budget can want opposite things from it: one to spend it all on the most benefit obtainable, another to spend as little of it as will do. Since the offer that wins differs between them while the affordability data does not distinguish them, a segmentation on spending power will place them together and mis-specify the offer for at least one.

scope.conditions: Presented as a generic Indian model applicable across consumer and industrial categories, on NCAER's consumer-classes framework as the underlying population data.

caveats.text: the claim that the model 'works for all businesses' is a strong universal, supported by a series of illustrative applications the author asserts rather than by any validation. No case is given where it failed, and no test is offered

the class labels (rich / consuming class / climbers / aspirants / destitute) come from NCAER; the VALUE-ORIENTATION overlay is the author's. The record keeps the two apart because the first is survey-derived and the second is not

the Nirma case that anchors the climbers segment is a well-known 1980s story told without figures beyond 'outselling it ten to one in tonnage terms', and the harshness of the product ('65 per cent soda ash') is reported as consumer-accepted on the basis of a single quoted rationalisation
population sizes attached to the segments are 2005-06 vintage and predate the period this project operates in

Evidential assessment recorded by the extractor, moved here from evidence.source_uncertainty when that field was returned to its controlled SPEC-03 vocabulary: The population data is named and sourced; the value-orientation overlay is the author's and is unvalidated.

source_stated_problems: a segmentation on spending power groups together buyers who want opposite things from the same budget
source_stated_remedies: segment on how the buyer trades benefit against cost, and design a portfolio spanning the resulting orientations

office automation: 'anywhere in the world' buyers, cost-benefit optimizing firms, fixed-budget grey-market buyers, and single shared assembled machines

item.question: What does the Woodward's Gripe Water calendar demonstrate, on this reading, and what is the general claim it supports?
item.answer: Jain reads M. V. Dhurandhar's 1932 calendar as deploying TWO DISTINCT REGISTERS OF SIGNIFICATION AT ONCE: a perspectival, narrative, allegorical register aimed at a modernising Indian and European resident elite, and an indexical, frontal, iconic register that institutes a divine presence. A single image addresses two constituencies that read pictures differently, without either being asked to read the other's way. The general claim it supports is that the deployment of new image-making techniques, including technological mass reproduction and elements of Western naturalism, 'helped mass-manufactured images to forge an arena of common address across varying social constituencies — that is, to "naturalize" an expanded category of the popular'. She states the consequence: 'commodity aesthetics provided a ground for reformulations of community and locality', driven by the opposing expansive and conservative imperatives of mass manufacture. This is an art-historical argument about a specific colonial episode, read from one image; it is not a general finding about how images address audiences.
item.support: new techniques 'helped mass-manufactured images to forge an arena of common address across varying social constituencies'
item.confounders: One image, closely read, is the whole evidence for this reading. The reading is careful and the evidential base is a single artefact.

results.representation_note: Q&A is an alternate grounded representation of the same source. It corroborates nothing on its own.
